title: Garba Season Is Back in Delhi: Where to Learn Dandiya Moves Ahead of Navratri
excerpt: Studios across Delhi and the NCR have opened festival-season batches with Sharad Navratri starting October 11 — from Rs 1,500-a-month group classes to weekend crash workshops.
body:
• Garba and dandiya classes are beginning across Delhi and the NCR as the city gears up for Sharad Navratri, which starts October 11 this year.
  • Sharad Navratri runs October 11–19, 2026, with Maha Navami on October 19 and Dussehra on October 20 — giving beginners about four weeks to learn the basics.
  • Studios typically offer festival-season batches, from group dance classes around Rs 1,500 a month to weekend workshops costing Rs 800–1,500.
  • Whether you want the traditional steps or just enough moves to survive a garba night, classes start well before the festival — sign-ups are open now.

Delhi's dance studios are filling up with an unusual crowd: accountants, college students and first-timers learning to move in circles. Garba and dandiya classes are beginning across the capital and the NCR, as the city prepares for Sharad Navratri — the nine-night festival honouring Goddess Durga that is also the year's biggest folk-dance season, according to Hindustan Times.

The Countdown Has Begun

Sharad Navratri 2026 begins on Sunday, October 11, with Ghatasthapana, and runs through Monday, October 19 (Maha Navami), followed by Vijayadashami or Dussehra on Tuesday, October 20. That gives beginners roughly four weeks to learn the fundamentals before the first garba night — which is exactly why studios start their festival batches now rather than in October.

Garba, the Gujarati folk dance performed in concentric circles around a lit lamp, and dandiya raas, its stick-based cousin, look effortless when done well. They are not. The footwork, the spins, the coordination with a partner's sticks — all of it takes practice, and the festival crowds are unforgiving.

What the Classes Teach

Festival-season batches typically start with the basics: the foundational three-step garba, rhythm and clapping patterns, and simple dandiya strikes, before moving to choreographed sequences that blend traditional steps with modern styling. Most studios run beginner and intermediate batches separately, with weekend batches for working professionals and weekday evening slots for students. Some studios also offer short pre-Navratri crash workshops — a single weekend of intensive training for the truly last-minute.

What It Costs

Prices vary widely by studio and format. Listings for dance classes in Delhi show regular group classes starting around Rs 1,500 a month — Stance Dance Studio in Jangpura lists dance classes at that price point — while established institutes like PAIPA in East of Kailash charge around Rs 4,000 for 8 sessions. Short festival workshops are priced by the day: a recent garba workshop in Delhi charged Rs 800 per day or Rs 1,500 for two days. Free introductory workshops also appear in the weeks before Navratri, as studios compete to fill their festival batches.

Where Delhi Learns

Studios across South, East and Central Delhi advertise garba batches each season — from large institutes to neighbourhood academies in Lajpat Nagar, Krishna Nagar and GTB Nagar, according to listings. Past seasons have also seen dedicated festive-season programming: Artist Dream Studio in Dwarka has run free garba workshops followed by regular paid batches, and outfits like SDDGM in Green Park and Lok Utsav in East Kidwai Nagar have organised pre-Navratri workshops. The pattern repeats every year, and this season is no different.

The Diaspora Angle

For Indians abroad, the Delhi garba rush is a reminder of how the festival travels. Garba nights now draw thousands in the US, UK and Canada every October, and many diaspora families time their India visits around the festival. Learning the steps in Delhi — or in a New Jersey community hall — is part of the same ritual: nine nights, one circle, and music that everybody knows.
